newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK March industrial production data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK March industrial production data.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to UK data showing March manufacturing output down 0.1 percent month-on-month and up 1.4 percent year-on-year, while overall industrial production was down 0.1 percent month-on-month and up 0.5 percent year-on-year.
"They are certainly weak and they confirm that sterling's strength is almost certainly beginning to impact on exports."

"They highlight the dichotomy between the manufacturing and service sector. In the end the Bank is going to side with the service sector and raise rates. It would be better to tighten on fiscal policy than raise rates and drive sterling through the roof but I think we will get more of tightening on the monetary side than the fiscal."

"It's a bit surprising because it's somewhat contrary to what we've been seeing in the survey data lately, which has been showing strong domestic demand for manufacturing goods actually offsetting the impact of the currency on demand for exports. It certainly seems to be that the currency is undermining demand for exports."

"The March figure is slightly weaker than expected but the monthly numbers do tend to be volatile. The underlying trend is still fairly buoyant, up 0.6 in the first quarter in line with the GDP projection. Talk of a split between the manufacturing and services sector is somewhat exaggerated. Classically the manufacturing sector lags the retail side. But we are beginning to see signs of a pick-up in response to the underlying strength of consumer demand. Monetary policy is far more potent than fiscal policy for controlling the economy. I think rates may need to go to around seven percent by the end of this year."

"These are a very weak set of figures, possibly indicating that sterling is hampering the manufacturing sector. This reduces the probability that we will see a near term rate rise. It brings out the dilema that faces policy makers and points to the need to tighten fiscal policy rather than use the interest rate weapon and further aggravate sterling strength. I don't think we will see another rate rise until September. In fiscal terms we're not expecting too much in terms of tightening until later this year. We don't know when the budget will be but when it comes we expect an increase in taxation of three bln pounds."
